I’m not exactly sure what my plan was. I think I just wanted to get him to listen to me. Look at me, properly. Like a friend, rather than a foe.

evidence.span:
“Ara,” I reply.


“Ara,” he repeats, flat.


“Yes.” I look at him funny, because he’s gone rigid. “What’s wrong with my name?”


“It’s an Old Rhavnan word for water.”


“I know.”


Ara actually, at its core, means a specific kind of water – warm, salty, nourishing seawater. The kind of water old Rhavnan ladies like to bathe in, believing it will cure all their ailments.


His mouth creases, like something has bothered him.


And then I get the ridiculous idea that actually, he might be blushing.


“It is…” he trails off.


“What?”


“My name is Drake.”


“Oh.”


His name means fire.


It’s very rare, and considered very good luck in Rhavnan tradition, to meet someone with a complimentary name to yours.


“Fate or chance?” he asks, with something like humour.


As Rhavnan people are highly superstitious, the answer to that often-asked question is almost always fate.


“Chance, probably. Although you can never meet my grandmother. She’d be planning a wedding.”


He says, half-smiling, “My mother would be, too.”


Just then, the sun seems to change. Becomes harsh. It’s catching his face in a different way, highlighting his deep-set eyes, his strong jaw.


I sit up swiftly. “You didn’t work at the Palace, did you? You look familiar.”


His smile fades fast.


“No. No, I’m from the west.”


I frown. “You don’t have a Banko accent.”


For some reason, that makes him laugh. Just once. It’s a strange sound, coming from him. I’d started to think he wasn’t capable of it.


Funny how the only time he’s laughed at something I’ve said is when it wasn’t a joke.


I wait, but he offers me nothing more, so I let it go. I suppose it wasn’t really my business anyway.


I suddenly find myself thinking about Eric. He must have made it home by now. But what if he’s hurt, or afraid?


“I need to go,” I state, fast. “I need to find my brother.”


“May I offer you some advice before you do? My way of paying my debt.”


“Yes?” I say, half expecting his advice to be something ridiculous.


It is.


“You should become a soldier. Your brother, too.”


“Are you being serious?”


“Unfortunately, I am.” He leans forwards. “The ship that fell today was a hive. Hives have their own fleet. They are fiercely protected. To go after one...” He pauses. “Hevalla must have known The Dragoness had something powerful in her possession.” He drops his voice, even though we’re still alone. “A weapon. And Hevalla used what must have been the majority of their fleets, across hive ships, to try to take it.”


“Did they manage to? Take it?”


“No. But for Hevalla to have had that knowledge…”


I understand. “Spies?”


He inspects the map in his hand.


“There was already talk of the Sky Treaty being broken. After today, I believe, for the first time in this war, the skies will be safer than the ground.”


“But—”


“Just think about it.”


He props his map on the table. I now have a clear view of it.


My village – in fact, most of the east coast of Hevalla – has been blotted out with ink.


Obliterated.


I’ve seen enough.  I jump out of the ship, my pulse frenzied.


“Wait,” he calls.


I turn.


“Dierai, Ara.”


I freeze like he’s just wrapped a hand around my heart.


“Dierai,” I choke out, in return.
